questions.stem: A 24 year old woman has a 6 month history of an intensely itchy rash on her neck and in both elbow creases. She had a similar rash as a child. She has hay fever every summer. The skin is dry, red and cracked, with scratch marks. Her temperature is 36.8°C and pulse rate 74 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Dry, itchy, cracked skin in the flexures with childhood onset and hay fever is atopic dermatitis persisting into adulthood.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: neck and in both elbow creases
steps.x: Flexural, itchy, dry rash with an atopic history.

elim: Contact dermatitis follows the site of an allergen, not the flexures since childhood.
Psoriasis has well-demarcated silvery plaques on extensor surfaces.
Scabies causes burrows in finger webs and spreads to contacts.
Seborrhoeic dermatitis affects the scalp, nasolabial folds and eyebrows with greasy scale.

steps.x: **B. Atopic dermatitis.** Flexures in older children and adults; atopy and childhood onset.

questions.stem: A 5 month old boy has a 3 week history of a red, dry, itchy rash on both cheeks, his scalp and the outer surfaces of his arms and legs. He rubs his face on the bedsheets and wakes at night. His nappy area is spared. His mother has asthma. He is feeding well and growing normally.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: In infants, atopic dermatitis affects the face, scalp and extensor surfaces; it is intensely itchy and usually spares the nappy area.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: both cheeks, his scalp and the outer surfaces
steps.x: Itchy rash on face, scalp and extensors in an infant with family atopy.

elim: Psoriasis in infants usually involves the nappy area with well-demarcated plaques.
The nappy area is spared.
Infant scabies affects palms, soles and spreads to family.
Cradle cap is greasy and not itchy, and the baby is not distressed.

steps.x: **A. Atopic dermatitis.** Infants: face/scalp/extensors. Children and adults: flexures.

questions.stem: A 13 year old girl has a 2 year history of an itchy rash behind both knees and in her elbow creases. She has asthma. Her GP is unsure whether this is eczema or psoriasis. Her temperature is 36.6°C. There are no nail changes and the scalp is clear.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination that supports atopic dermatitis?
o: Pinpoint bleeding when scale is removed
Well-demarcated plaques on the extensor surfaces
questions.e: In atopic dermatitis the erythema is poorly demarcated, unlike the sharply demarcated plaques of psoriasis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: behind both knees and in her elbow creases
steps.x: Flexural rash; the question is eczema versus psoriasis.

elim: That is plaque psoriasis.
Nail changes suggest psoriasis, and she has none.
That is the Auspitz sign of psoriasis.
That is psoriasis.

steps.x: **D. Poorly demarcated red, dry patches.** Eczema: poorly demarcated. Psoriasis: well demarcated.

questions.stem: An 8 month old girl with atopic eczema has a 1 day history of a rapidly spreading rash over her trunk and her eczema patches. There are many uniform, small, punched-out erosions and some blisters. She is miserable and feeding poorly. Her temperature is 38.7°C and pulse rate 162 bpm. Her father has a cold sore.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Widespread monomorphic punched-out erosions over eczema with fever, and a contact with a cold sore, is eczema herpeticum from HSV-1. In babies it can affect the trunk.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Monomorphic erosions plus fever plus HSV contact.

elim: Impetigo causes golden crusts or large bullae, not uniform punched-out erosions with fever.
Chickenpox lesions are at different stages, not monomorphic over eczema.
A flare does not cause fever and punched-out erosions.
SSSS causes widespread erythema and sheet-like peeling.

steps.x: **C. Eczema herpeticum.** Eczema herpeticum: HSV-1, monomorphic blisters/erosions, fever, malaise.

questions.stem: A 3 year old boy with atopic eczema has a 2 day history of blisters over his eczema on his hands and around his mouth, with fever. Several children at his nursery have hand, foot and mouth disease. He was started on IV aciclovir for presumed eczema herpeticum but after 48 hours there is no improvement. HSV PCR is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Eczema coxsackium mimics eczema herpeticum after hand, foot and mouth disease contact, and does not respond to IV aciclovir.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
HFMD contact, HSV negative, no aciclovir response.

elim: HSV PCR is negative and there is no response to aciclovir.
Molluscum causes pearly umbilicated papules without fever.
S. aureus causes golden crusting, not vesicles after hand, foot and mouth contact.
Chickenpox is generalised and responds to aciclovir.

steps.x: **A. Coxsackievirus.** Coxsackievirus causes eczema coxsackium, which does not respond to aciclovir.

questions.stem: A 4 year old girl has had atopic eczema since she was 6 months old. Her father has hay fever and her brother has asthma. Her mother asks which other condition she is most at risk of developing as she grows up. Her eczema is well controlled with emollients.
questions.q: Which condition is she most likely to develop?
questions.e: Eczema, asthma and allergic rhinitis form the atopic triad; children with eczema and a family history of atopy are at high risk of allergic rhinitis and asthma.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: atopic eczema since she was 6 months old
steps.x: Eczema plus strong family atopy.

elim: Coeliac disease is autoimmune and not part of the atopic triad.
Psoriasis is not part of the atopic triad.
Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune, not atopic.
Vitiligo is autoimmune, not atopic.

steps.x: **A. Allergic rhinitis.** Atopic triad: eczema, asthma, allergic rhinitis.

questions.stem: A 6 year old boy is seen with a 3 month history of an itchy, dry rash. His GP applies the NICE criteria for atopic eczema. He has had an itchy skin condition, visible flexural dermatitis, and generally dry skin. His parents are not sure about the rest of his history.
questions.q: Which additional feature in his history would best support the diagnosis?
o: Onset before the age of 2 years
Rash only on the palms and soles
questions.e: NICE criteria for atopic eczema in under 12s include onset before age 2, along with flexural involvement, dry skin and a personal history of atopy.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
He meets itch, flexures and dry skin; one more criterion is needed.

elim: Fever suggests infection, not eczema.
That is seborrhoeic dermatitis.
That suggests pompholyx or contact dermatitis.
That is psoriasis.

steps.x: **C. Onset before the age of 2 years.** NICE CG57: itch plus flexural rash, dry skin, atopy, onset before age 2.

questions.stem: A 32 year old man has had atopic eczema since childhood that has been well controlled. Over the last 3 weeks it has flared on his trunk and arms. He recently changed to a cheaper biological washing powder and uses a new perfumed shower gel. He has no new pets. His temperature is 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely trigger for this flare?
questions.e: Soaps and detergents are classic eczema triggers; his flare followed a new washing powder and perfumed shower gel.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
New irritants on the skin before the flare.

elim: Antibiotics do not trigger eczema flares.
HSV causes eczema herpeticum with fever and erosions, not a gradual flare.
New food allergy is unlikely to start in adulthood.
Streptococcal infection triggers guttate psoriasis.

steps.x: **D. Soaps and detergents.** Triggers: soaps/detergents, dust mites, cold weather, stress, foods.

questions.stem: A 7 year old boy with severe atopic eczema since infancy also has allergic rhinitis and recently developed wheeze. His paediatrician sends blood tests. His temperature is 36.8°C and pulse rate 92 bpm. His eczema involves both elbow and knee flexures.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on blood tests?
questions.e: Atopic dermatitis is associated with raised IgE, driven by a Th2 hypersensitivity response to allergens penetrating the damaged barrier.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Full atopic picture.

elim: Low complement suggests lupus or nephritis.
IgA deficiency is not the classic finding.
That is coeliac disease.
ANA suggests connective tissue disease.

steps.x: **E. Raised total IgE.** Atopy: Th2-driven, raised IgE.

questions.stem: A 10 year old girl with atopic eczema has a 3 day history of her eczema on both hands becoming wet and sore, with honey-coloured crusts. She is otherwise well. Her temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 88 bpm. There are no punched-out erosions or blisters. A swab is sent.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Weeping eczema with honey-coloured crusts in a well child is secondary bacterial infection, typically S. aureus, treated with flucloxacillin.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: wet and sore, with honey-coloured crusts
steps.x: Crusting, weeping, afebrile, no erosions.

elim: That does not produce honey-coloured crusts.
Coxsackium causes vesicles with fever after HFMD contact.
There are no punched-out erosions and she is well.
Pompholyx causes deep itchy vesicles on palms, not crusts.

steps.x: **E. Secondary bacterial infection of eczema.** Infected eczema: usually S. aureus; give flucloxacillin.

questions.stem: A 9 year old boy of Black African heritage has had a potent topical corticosteroid applied to eczema on his arms for 3 months without breaks. His mother now notices pale patches where the cream was applied. The patches are not itchy or scaly. His eczema is controlled. He is otherwise well.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of the pale patches?
questions.e: Topical corticosteroids can cause depigmentation by inhibiting melanocytes, which is more visible in darker skin types.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Pale patches exactly where steroid was used on darker skin.

elim: Lichen sclerosus affects the genital skin.
Pityriasis versicolor is scaly and on the trunk.
Tinea forms itchy scaly rings.
Vitiligo is not confined to where the steroid was applied.

steps.x: **A. Depigmentation from topical corticosteroid.** Topical steroids can depigment darker skin.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man with lifelong atopic eczema and asthma has a 2 day history of painful, clustered, punched-out sores spreading across his face and neck over his eczema. He kissed a partner with a cold sore last week. He feels unwell and shivery. His temperature is 38.4°C and pulse rate 108 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Eczema herpeticum is a severe HSV-1 complication of eczema: painful monomorphic punched-out erosions with fever and malaise.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Monomorphic erosions, HSV contact, systemically unwell.

elim: Acne causes comedones and pustules, not punched-out erosions with fever.
Impetigo has golden crusts and the patient is usually well.
Shingles is dermatomal and unilateral.
Rosacea is chronic and not febrile.

steps.x: **B. Eczema herpeticum.** Eczema herpeticum is an emergency in adults and children alike.

questions.stem: A 15 year old girl has had an itchy, dry rash since early childhood that comes and goes. It is always worse in winter and around exams. It affects her neck and the fronts of her elbows, where the skin is now thickened with accentuated skin lines. She has asthma. Her temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A chronic relapsing itchy flexural rash with lichenification, flaring with cold weather and stress, in an asthmatic is atopic dermatitis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: worse in winter and around exams
steps.x: Chronic with flares, triggers, lichenification, atopy.

elim: Contact dermatitis follows an allergen site, not a lifelong flexural pattern.
Lichen planus causes purple, polygonal papules on wrists.
Psoriasis favours extensor surfaces with silvery scale.
Tinea is an annular scaly patch.

steps.x: **B. Atopic dermatitis.** Chronic inflammatory condition with flare-ups and lichenification.

questions.stem: A 6 year old boy with atopic eczema has flares each time he stays at his grandmother's house, which has thick carpets and old feather pillows. His eczema settles within a week of returning home. He has no pets at home and no food allergies. His temperature is 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely trigger for his flares?
questions.e: House dust mites, found in carpets and bedding, are a recognised trigger for atopic eczema.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: thick carpets and old feather pillows
settles within a week of returning home
steps.x: Flares with carpets and old bedding.

elim: The flares follow the carpets and bedding, not swimming.
The flares are linked to a place, not the season.
He has no food allergies.
Pollen is seasonal and outdoor.

steps.x: **D. House dust mite.** Triggers: dust mites, soaps, cold, stress, foods.

questions.stem: A 10 month old girl has had a dry, itchy rash on her cheeks and the fronts of her knees for 2 months. Her father has asthma. She is growing well. Her parents ask for a test to prove what the rash is before starting treatment. Her temperature is 36.9°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Atopic dermatitis is a clinical diagnosis in most cases; no test is needed to confirm typical eczema.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the question being asked.

clues: cheeks and the fronts of her knees
a test to prove what the rash is
steps.x: Typical infant distribution and family atopy.

elim: IgE may be raised but does not confirm eczema.
Biopsy is invasive and not needed for typical eczema.
Patch testing is for suspected contact allergy.
Nothing suggests a fungal rash.

steps.x: **A. No investigation: clinical diagnosis.** Eczema is diagnosed clinically.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman has had atopic eczema since childhood. Over 4 months she has developed eczema on her earlobes and wrist where she wears costume jewellery and a metal-backed watch. Her flexural eczema is unchanged. Her temperature is 36.6°C and pulse rate 70 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Skin patch testing is used when a trigger or allergic contact dermatitis is suspected, here nickel in jewellery.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the question being asked.

clues: costume jewellery and a metal-backed watch
steps.x: New eczema where metal touches the skin.

elim: A contact allergen is suspected and can be identified.
IgE does not identify a contact allergen.
Biopsy will not identify the allergen.
Prick testing detects immediate IgE allergy, not contact dermatitis.

steps.x: **D. Skin patch testing.** Suspected allergic contact dermatitis: patch test.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man with atopic eczema has used the same emollient for years. Over 2 months his eczema has worsened wherever he applies a new perfumed cream recommended by a friend, with redness and itching strictly at those sites. His temperature is 36.8°C. He wants to know which ingredient is responsible.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Patch testing identifies the ingredient causing allergic contact dermatitis when a trigger is suspected.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the question being asked.
Reaction only where the new product touches.

elim: Food IgE does not identify a cream allergen.
Biopsy will not identify the allergen.
There are no features of infection.
There are no blisters or erosions.

steps.x: **C. Skin patch testing.** Allergy/patch testing if a trigger or contact dermatitis is suspected.

questions.stem: A 4 year old girl with atopic eczema is brought to her GP with a 1 day history of painful, clustered, punched-out erosions on her face. She is lethargic. Her temperature is 38.5°C and pulse rate 140 bpm. The GP suspects eczema herpeticum.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in her assessment?
o: Prescribe oral flucloxacillin and review in 48 hours
Start hydrocortisone 1% and review in 1 week
questions.e: Suspected eczema herpeticum needs immediate hospital referral for same-day dermatology assessment and IV aciclovir.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the question being asked.
Suspected eczema herpeticum in primary care.

elim: This is not bacterial and needs same-day specialist care.
Routine referral is far too slow.
Patch testing has no role in an acute infection.
Steroid alone can worsen HSV spread.

steps.x: **C. Same-day dermatology assessment in hospital.** Eczema herpeticum: same-day dermatology assessment / immediate referral.

questions.stem: A 3 month old boy has mild dry, itchy patches on his cheeks and arms. There is no weeping, crusting or broken skin. He feeds well. His parents bathe him daily with bubble bath. His temperature is 36.8°C. The GP diagnoses mild atopic eczema.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Emollients and stop the bubble bath
questions.e: Basic skin care with emollients is first-line, with soap substitutes in place of irritants like bubble bath.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.

clues: no weeping, crusting or broken skin
steps.x: Mild eczema with an irritant in use.

elim: Antihistamines are not first-line for eczema.
There is no infection.
Moderate potency is not needed for mild infant eczema.
Calcineurin inhibitors are for severe disease.

steps.x: **A. Emollients and stop the bubble bath.** First-line: emollients (e.g. Epaderm, Diprobase, Cetraben).

questions.stem: A 7 year old boy with atopic eczema uses an emollient twice daily. He now has a flare with red, dry, itchy patches on his eyelids and cheeks and in his neck folds. There is no infection. His temperature is 36.7°C and pulse rate 88 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment to add?
questions.e: A mild-potency topical corticosteroid such as hydrocortisone 1% is used for flares, especially on the face and flexures, per NICE.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.

clues: eyelids and cheeks and in his neck folds
steps.x: Facial flare in a child, no infection.

elim: Potent steroids should be avoided on the face.
Very potent steroids are not used on a child's face.
There is no HSV infection.
Systemic steroids are not used for a facial flare.

steps.x: **C. Hydrocortisone 1% cream.** Face/flexures: mild potency (hydrocortisone 1%).

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman has a flare of moderate atopic eczema on her forearms and shins with excoriations from scratching. There is no weeping or crusting. Emollients alone have not settled it. She has no facial involvement. Her temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Emollient alone at a higher frequency
questions.e: Moderate eczema with excoriations on the limbs is treated with emollients plus a short course of moderate-potency steroid such as clobetasone butyrate 0.05%.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
Moderate flare on limbs, emollient has failed.

elim: Emollient alone has already failed.
There is no eczema herpeticum.
Systemic therapy is for severe refractory disease.
Calcineurin inhibitors are for severe disease.

steps.x: **B. Emollient with short-term clobetasone butyrate 0.05%.** Moderate: emollient + clobetasone butyrate 0.05%.

questions.stem: A 2 year old boy has severe, widespread atopic eczema that keeps him awake despite regular emollients and a topical corticosteroid. There is no sign of infection. The dermatology nurse wants to maximise the effect of his topical treatment overnight. His temperature is 36.8°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional measure?
questions.e: Wet wrapping over emollient and steroid maximises their effect in severe childhood eczema.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.

clues: maximise the effect of his topical treatment
steps.x: Severe childhood eczema, topicals need boosting.

elim: Bubble baths are irritants.
There is no infection.
Dietary exclusion is not routine.
Not appropriate for a toddler.

steps.x: **E. Wet wrapping.** Wet wrapping maximises effect in severe childhood eczema.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man has severe atopic eczema on his trunk and limbs. It has not been controlled with emollients, potent topical corticosteroids, wet wraps and then 3 months of topical tacrolimus. It affects his sleep and university work. His temperature is 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Refer to dermatology for systemic therapy
Stop all treatment and review in 3 months
questions.e: Severe eczema uses topical calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus and may progress to systemic therapy when these fail.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
Severe disease, failed topical steroids and tacrolimus.

elim: A weaker steroid will not help severe disease.
There is no infection.
No contact allergen is suspected.
Leaving severe eczema untreated is inappropriate.

steps.x: **C. Refer to dermatology for systemic therapy.** Severe: tacrolimus/pimecrolimus, then systemic therapy.

questions.stem: A 12 year old girl has severe atopic eczema on her eyelids and around her mouth. Emollients and hydrocortisone 1% have not controlled it. She has thin skin on her eyelids already, and her parents want to avoid stronger steroids on her face. She is otherwise well.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus or pimecrolimus) treat severe eczema without steroid skin thinning, ideal for the face and eyelids.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
Severe facial eczema, steroid-sparing wanted.

elim: Very potent steroid on eyelids risks atrophy.
Systemic steroid is not appropriate.
There is no fungal infection.
Not used on the face.

steps.x: **D. Topical pimecrolimus.** Topical calcineurin inhibitor for severe facial eczema.

questions.stem: A 6 year old girl's atopic eczema is now clear after a flare treated with hydrocortisone 1%. Her mother asks how best to prevent further flares. She bathes her daily. Her temperature is 36.6°C and her skin is mildly dry.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Apply emollient only when the rash returns
Apply emollient regularly, including after bathing
questions.e: Long-term, regular emollients hydrate the skin and prevent flares, applied after a bath or shower.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
Prevention, not treating a flare.

elim: Emollients should continue when skin is clear.
Steroids are for flares, not continuous use.
Dietary exclusion is not routine.
Soap is an irritant.

steps.x: **B. Apply emollient regularly, including after bathing.** Long term: regular emollients after bath/shower.

questions.stem: A 22 year old woman with atopic eczema has a 1 day history of painful, monomorphic punched-out erosions on her neck and chest over her eczema. She feels feverish and unwell. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. She is admitted.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Eczema herpeticum (HSV-1) is treated with IV aciclovir.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
Eczema herpeticum, systemically unwell.

elim: This is viral, not bacterial.
Steroids can worsen HSV spread.
Steroids will not treat HSV.
Immunomodulators may worsen infection.

steps.x: **A. IV aciclovir.** Eczema herpeticum: IV aciclovir.

questions.stem: An 11 year old boy with atopic eczema has a 4 day history of weeping, crusted eczema on his legs. A skin swab grows Staphylococcus aureus. He is well, with temperature 37.2°C and pulse rate 90 bpm. He has no drug allergies. There are no blisters or erosions.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Secondary bacterial infection of eczema is typically S. aureus and is treated with flucloxacillin.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
Infected eczema, S. aureus, no allergy.

elim: Clotrimazole treats fungal, not bacterial, infection.
This is bacterial, not HSV.
Metronidazole does not cover S. aureus well.
This is not a fungal infection.

steps.x: **B. Flucloxacillin.** Secondary bacterial infection: flucloxacillin.

questions.stem: A GP plans to prescribe a 2 week course of a moderate-potency topical corticosteroid for a 28 year old woman of South Asian heritage with a flare of atopic eczema on her forearms. She asks what side effects she should look out for. She is otherwise well.
questions.q: Which side effect is most important to warn her about?
o: Excess hair growth on the scalp
questions.e: Topical corticosteroids can cause depigmentation in darker skin types, which patients should be warned about.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
Topical steroid in darker skin.

elim: Not a typical effect of steroid on the forearm.
Not a recognised effect.
Topical use rarely causes systemic effects.
Not a classic effect of topical steroids.

steps.x: **B. Depigmentation of the treated skin.** Topical steroids can depigment darker skin.

questions.stem: A 4 year old boy has severely dry, itchy skin and eczema since infancy. Genetic testing shows a loss-of-function mutation in the filaggrin gene. His mother asks why his skin dries out so quickly even after a bath. His temperature is 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his dry skin?
questions.e: Filaggrin loss impairs stratum corneum formation, weakening the barrier and increasing transepidermal water loss and allergen entry.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding to the mechanism behind it.

clues: loss-of-function mutation in the filaggrin gene
steps.x: Faulty barrier protein, dry skin.

elim: Sebum is not the problem.
Sweating would make skin moist.
Not the mechanism.
Melanin does not hold water.

steps.x: **C. Increased transepidermal water loss.** Filaggrin loss: weak barrier, more water loss, more allergen entry.

questions.stem: A 9 year old girl with atopic eczema has a raised total IgE and positive specific IgE to house dust mite. Her immunologist explains that allergens are crossing her damaged skin barrier and stimulating a particular arm of the immune system. Her temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which immune response is most responsible for her chronic skin inflammation?
questions.e: Allergens penetrating the defective barrier trigger a Th2-mediated hypersensitivity response, driving chronic inflammation and raised IgE.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding to the mechanism behind it.
Allergens across the barrier and raised IgE.

elim: Not the mechanism.
That causes vasculitis and nephritis.
That is TB or sarcoidosis.
That is the main axis in psoriasis.

steps.x: **E. Th2-mediated hypersensitivity.** Eczema: Th2. Psoriasis: Th17/IL-23.

questions.stem: A 6 year old boy had atopic eczema from 3 months of age, developed a peanut allergy at 2 and now has asthma. His mother asks why he keeps developing new allergic conditions. His eczema is controlled with emollients. He is otherwise well.
questions.q: Which is the best explanation?
o: Atopic march from shared genetic and immunological predisposition
questions.e: Eczema, food allergy, asthma and allergic rhinitis appear in sequence in the atopic march, reflecting a shared genetic and immunological predisposition.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding to the mechanism behind it.
Allergic conditions appearing in sequence.

elim: Infections do not explain this sequence.
Emollients do not cause asthma.
Steroids do not cause atopy.
These conditions are linked.

steps.x: **A. Atopic march from shared genetic and immunological predisposition.** Atopic march: shared predisposition.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man has had atopic eczema since childhood. He scratches the back of his neck every evening. The skin there is now thickened, leathery and grey with exaggerated skin markings. There is no scale. His temperature is 36.5°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the skin thickening?
o: Fungal invasion of the stratum corneum
questions.e: Lichenification results from repeated mechanical trauma of scratching driving keratinocyte proliferation and epidermal thickening.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding to the mechanism behind it.

clues: scratches the back of his neck every evening
steps.x: Lichenification at a scratched site.

elim: That causes thinning, not thickening.
Not fungal; there is no scale.
That causes vitiligo.
